title: Subroutines
body:
Functions, before anything makes them easy. Two instructions do the mechanical part:

- `jsr label` pushes the return address (the PC) onto the stack, then jumps.
- `rts` pops it back into the PC.

`bsr` is the same as `jsr` but PC-relative and shorter, exactly as `bra` is to `jmp`.

Everything else about a function call, arguments, return values, which registers survive, is
**convention, not hardware**. The 68000 will happily let you get it wrong.

## The stack

`a7` is the stack pointer, and it has an alias, `sp`. It grows *downwards*: pushing
decrements it. That is why push and pop are written as [[Addressing Modes|addressing modes]]
rather than instructions:

```
move.l  d0,-(sp)     ; push: pre-decrement
move.l  (sp)+,d0     ; pop:  post-increment
movem.l d0-d3/a0-a1,-(sp)   ; push several at once
movem.l (sp)+,d0-d3/a0-a1   ; and restore, same order
```

`movem` is the one to reach for when saving registers around a call, because it is one
instruction and it keeps the order straight for you.

Note `a7` is really two registers: the user stack pointer and the supervisor stack pointer,
and which one you get depends on the mode bit. See [[Supervisor State]].

## Calling conventions

The two that matter here:

- **Registers.** Put arguments in `d0`, `d1`, `a0`; return in `d0`. Fast, no memory traffic,
  but you run out of registers and it makes recursion awkward.
- **Stack.** Push arguments before the `jsr`, read them back at fixed offsets from `sp`,
  and have the caller clean up afterwards. This is what C does, and what [[System Call]]
  traps expect.

The stack version needs care about the offsets, because the return address is sitting on top
of the arguments:

```
        move.w  #5,-(sp)        ; argument
        jsr     twice
        addq.l  #2,sp           ; caller cleans up

twice:  move.w  4(sp),d0        ; 0(sp) is the return address, 4(sp) is the arg
        add.w   d0,d0
        rts                     ; result in d0
```

## Stack frames and why recursion works

A **stack frame** is one call's private block on the stack: return address, saved registers,
arguments, and locals. Because each call pushes its own, a function can be executing several
times at once without the copies interfering, which is the whole mechanism behind
[[Recursion]]. `link`/`unlk` build and tear down a frame using `a6` as a frame pointer, so
locals get stable offsets even as the stack pointer moves.

This is the concrete version of the stack half of [[Stack and Heap]] from
[[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]], and it is also where stack overflow comes from:
infinite recursion pushes frames until `a7` walks off the end of memory and you get a bus
error.

## Ways to get it wrong

- Pushing and not popping, or popping a different size than you pushed. The `rts` then
  returns to whatever garbage is on top, and you land in data: illegal instruction, four
  bombs. See [[Assembly Errors]].
- Clobbering a register the caller was using. Save it with `movem` or document that you
  do not.
- Forgetting the caller-cleanup `addq` after a stack-argument call, which leaks the stack a
  few bytes per call until a loop kills you.
